_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 4 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 1 Loops in Algorithms. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order (a loop; count-controlled and its counter; forever; a wrong step inside a loop; concise; the third kind of loop), in the lesson's own examples: the watering can, the teeth and the traffic lights. Every expansion and every turn count is taken from the lesson's OWN rules through the adapter - ART.algo.flatten for the turns of a repeat and a forever box, ART.algo.expandLoop for the nine and twelve steps written out - so a count in this film cannot disagree with the lesson that runs it.
title: Loops in Algorithms
subtitle: Grade 4 Computing
objectives: Follow, understand, edit and correct algorithms that use repetition, including indefinite (forever) loops.
Follow, understand, edit and correct algorithms that use iteration, including count-controlled loops.
Understand that the use of repetition can make algorithms more concise.

beats.say: Repeat four times: brush the top, brush the bottom. Round and round it goes.
That is a loop. A loop can count its turns, or never stop at all.
A loop is a part of an algorithm that happens again and again.
These three steps water one plant. Fill the can, pour on a plant, walk to the next.
When you reach the last step in the loop, you go back to the first.
And you keep count of the turns. This loop goes round three times.
Repeat four times: brush the top, brush the bottom. Then rinse.
A count-controlled loop has something you cannot see. It has a counter.
The counter starts at one, and goes up by one every time round.
When the counter reaches four, the loop stops. Then you rinse.
That is iteration with a count-controlled loop.
Two steps, four turns. That is eight brushing steps in all.
Traffic lights run a loop too. Red, red and amber, green, amber.
The box says forever. There is no count in it at all.
So the loop has no end of its own. Something outside has to stop it.
A switch, a person, a power cut. That is an indefinite loop.
Forever does not mean broken. Clocks and games are meant to keep going.
A wrong step outside a loop goes wrong once. Inside, it goes wrong every turn.
Repeat three times: fill the can, pour on a plant, tip the can upside down.
Tipping the can empties it on the floor, every time round.
Change that one step to walk to the next plant.
One fix inside the loop, and all three turns are fixed.
Fill, pour, walk, three times over, is nine steps written out.
Repeat three times, fill, pour, walk, is three steps and a count.
Shorter to read, and shorter to write. You see it all at once.
Four plants instead of three? Change the three to a four.

at.change: Change the three to a four

beats.say: Written out long, you would add three more steps. A loop is concise.
There is a third kind of loop, waiting for you in Scratch.
A condition-controlled loop has no count, but it does have an end.
It goes round until something becomes true. Repeat until the down arrow is pressed.
One stops after a number, one when something happens, and forever never stops.
A loop is a part of an algorithm that happens again and again.
A count-controlled loop has a counter. It counts its turns, then stops.
A forever loop has no counter, so something outside has to stop it.
And a loop is concise: written once, done many times.
